say.text: Mixed quiz. The first five have hints; the last five are cold. Answer from what you already hold.
Of all peptic ulcer perforations, where does the hole most often lie? Consider the stomach and the first part of the duodenum.

choices.label: Anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum
Posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Anterior duodenal ulcers erode forward and perforate. Posterior ones erode the gastroduodenal artery behind them and bleed.
Yes. The anterior wall faces the free peritoneal cavity, so erosion through it perforates.

choices.label: I know this, skip the recap

say.text: That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the posterior wall is the one that bleeds, so it feels like the dangerous site. Ask what lies behind each wall.

sure_note.text: You were sure the posterior wall is the dangerous one; test what lies behind each wall.

say.text: Posterior ulcers bleed because the gastroduodenal artery runs behind the duodenum and gets eroded. Anterior ulcers perforate into the free belly, so the anterior wall is the commonest site.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because lesser curvature ulcers are a familiar stomach site. Check which site the classic teaching names as the commonest.

sure_note.text: You were sure the lesser curvature is the commonest site; re-check the duodenal site.

say.text: The lesser curvature is a stomach site, but the classic commonest site of perforation is the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum.
Ask which wall faces the free peritoneal cavity, and which wall sits over a large artery.
Same region, a different case.
A man with melaena has a bleeding ulcer on the first part of the duodenum. Which wall did it sit on, and which artery did it erode?

choices.label: Front wall of the first part; gastroduodenal artery eroded
Back wall of the first part; left gastric artery eroded
Not sure, give me a hint
Back wall of the first part; gastroduodenal artery eroded

say.text: Yes. Posterior ulcers bleed because they erode the gastroduodenal artery that runs behind the first part of the duodenum.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting to pair the famous front-wall site with the artery, since it is the site everyone remembers. Check which wall bleeding ulcers erode from.

sure_note.text: You were sure the front wall is the bleeder; re-check which wall faces the belly.

say.text: The front wall perforates because it faces the free peritoneal cavity; it does not bleed from the gastroduodenal artery. The back wall bleeds by eroding that artery.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the back wall is right and the left gastric artery is a real stomach artery. Name the artery that runs behind the duodenum.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the artery; check which vessel lies behind the first part of the duodenum.

say.text: The left gastric artery supplies the stomach, not the duodenal wall. The gastroduodenal artery runs behind the first part of the duodenum, and a posterior ulcer erodes it.
Think about which wall lies behind the duodenum and which artery runs there, not which wall faces the belly.
A man has peritonitis and free gas on his erect film, with no other clue to the cause.
What is the best reading of that gas?

choices.label: A perforated ulcer, since no other cause is ever seen
Not sure, give me a hint
Most likely a perforated ulcer, though not the only cause
A perforated ulcer, because free gas always means one

say.text: Yes. A perforated ulcer is the most common cause of pneumoperitoneum. That is a frequency, so other causes still exist.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the commonest cause feels like the only cause you need to name. Check what 'commonest' promises.

sure_note.text: You were sure one kind of free gas means one cause; test that rule.

say.text: Perforated ulcer is the commonest cause of pneumoperitoneum, a frequency, not a rule. Free gas always needs the clinical picture and other causes kept in mind.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the ulcer is the most familiar cause, so other causes seem never to show up. Check whether a frequency can rule them out.

sure_note.text: You were sure no other cause appears; a frequency cannot establish that.

say.text: Other causes do occur, so the commonest cause does not exclude them. The statement is about frequency, and the ulcer remains the most likely reading.
Ask what 'commonest' promises, and whether a frequency can rule out every other cause.
A film shows haustral markings in gas lying between the liver and the diaphragm, in a man with no peritonism.
Which name fits this sign?

choices.label: Chilaiditi sign, colon between liver and diaphragm
Rigler's sign, gas on both sides of a bowel wall
Football sign, gas outlining the whole abdomen
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Yes. In the Chilaiditi sign the colon sits under the diaphragm, and its haustra show the gas is inside bowel, not free.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because Rigler's is a real sign on films, so a gas shadow near the dome seems to fit it. Check what the gas is inside.

sure_note.text: You were sure a real free-gas sign fits; check whether the gas sits inside a loop.

say.text: Rigler's sign is gas on both sides of a bowel wall, which marks free gas in the peritoneal cavity. Haustral markings show this gas is inside the colon, so it is pseudo-pneumoperitoneum.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the football sign is a dramatic free-gas picture, and any gas high in the abdomen looks like it. Ask whether the gas outlines the belly or sits in one loop.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the free-gas picture; check whether this gas outlines the belly at all.

say.text: The football sign is gas outlining the whole abdomen, a true free-gas pattern. This film shows gas in one colon loop with haustra, so the Chilaiditi sign fits.
Ask whether the gas is inside the bowel or outside it, and whether the colon could be the thing lying there.
A registrar says: 'CT is always the first test in a belly like this, so skip the film.'
Which reply is correct?

choices.label: Agree: CT is first, since it is the most sensitive test
Agree in part: the erect film is the most sensitive test
Not sure, give me a hint
Erect chest X-ray first; CT if the film is equivocal

say.text: Yes. The erect film is the usual first test and shows free gas in about three-quarters of cases. CT is the most sensitive test, reserved for an equivocal film.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because CT is the most sensitive test, so it feels like the right first test. Ask whether sensitive and first are the same question.

sure_note.text: You were sure the most sensitive test is the first test; separate the two questions.

say.text: CT abdomen is the most sensitive test and the choice when the X-ray is equivocal. First and most sensitive are separate questions; the erect chest X-ray is the usual first test.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the erect film is the test you order first, so it feels like the best test as well. Check which test is most sensitive.

sure_note.text: You were sure the first test is also the best; check which test ranks higher on sensitivity.

say.text: The erect film is the usual first test, not the most sensitive. CT abdomen is the most sensitive investigation and the choice when the film is equivocal.
Treat first and most sensitive as two separate questions. Which test would you order at the front door?
Second half: no hints. Commit to one answer each time.
A 45-year-old has a rigid belly. The night team reads his erect film as clear and proposes discharge. What should happen before he goes home?

choices.label: Repeat the erect film at the morning round
CT abdomen before any discharge, given the rigidity
Discharge on oral analgesia with clinic review

say.text: Yes. A clear erect film does not exclude perforation: about a quarter of perforations show no free gas, so a rigid belly needs CT first.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because a clear film feels reassuring, and oral analgesia looks like a safe plan. Ask what a rigid belly means while the film is clear.

sure_note.text: You were sure the clear film settles it; a quarter of perforations show no gas.

say.text: A clear film does not exclude perforation, because free gas is absent in a sizeable minority. A rigid belly still needs CT before he goes home.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because a morning repeat sounds cautious and cheap. Ask whether a repeat film can rule out what the first film missed.

sure_note.text: You were sure a repeat film would settle it; the same test can miss gas again.

say.text: Repeating the same film only repeats the test that can miss free gas. CT is the test that settles it when the belly is rigid.
A man with a perforated ulcer arrives shocked, with a rigid belly and a systolic pressure in the 80s.
What is the first action?

choices.label: Large-bore IV access, crystalloid and nasogastric tube
Straight to laparotomy, since the cause is known
CT abdomen first, while fluids wait for the scan

say.text: Yes. Resuscitation comes first so he survives theatre. Antibiotics and an IV PPI start on diagnosis.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the operation is the definitive treatment, so it feels like the urgent step. Ask what keeps him alive until he reaches theatre.

sure_note.text: You were sure the operation comes first; fluids come before the definitive step.

say.text: Theatre is the definitive step, but a shocked patient must be resuscitated first. Fluids, a nasogastric tube and monitoring come before the operation.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because the scan answers the diagnosis, which seems to come first. Ask whether the diagnosis is still in doubt in this patient.

sure_note.text: You were sure imaging comes first; fluids and antibiotics do not wait for the scan.

say.text: The diagnosis is clear enough to act on, and a scan that delays fluids is the wrong order. Resuscitation and antibiotics start first; imaging only if the diagnosis is still in doubt.
Two patients with a perforated ulcer are being planned for management.
Which one fits non-operative (Taylor) management?

choices.label: Stable patient with free gas on the erect film
Elderly steroid user, generalised peritonitis, steady pulse
Stable case with a contained leak shown on contrast

say.text: Yes. Taylor management suits a selected stable patient whose perforation is contained and confirmed on a water-soluble study.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because stability feels like the only condition, and free gas is already visible. Ask what must be shown before conservative care.

sure_note.text: You were sure stability is enough; check what must be shown first.

say.text: Stability alone is not enough: Taylor management needs a contained perforation confirmed on contrast. Free gas is a reason to check the seal, not to start conservative care.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because a steady pulse looks like a patient who is coping. Ask whether generalised peritonitis fits a selected, contained case.

sure_note.text: You were sure a steady pulse makes conservative care safe; generalised peritonitis is the exclusion.

say.text: Generalised peritonitis is not a contained perforation, so the Taylor method does not fit. He needs resuscitation and surgical repair.
A woman had a sudden perforation ten hours ago.
Now she is sitting up, eating a biscuit and says the pain has gone. Her abdomen is still tender and her pulse is 116. What is the best reading?

choices.label: Spontaneous healing, so surgery can wait until morning
False calm, the reaction phase before bacterial spread
Real recovery, so she can move to the ward tonight

say.text: Yes. The pain eases as dilute exudate settles, but bacteria follow over hours. A tender belly and a fast pulse fit that.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because she looks better and asks for food, which is what recovery looks like. Ask what a tender belly and a fast pulse suggest.

sure_note.text: You were sure she is recovering; the easing of pain is the phase that misleads.

say.text: Relief of pain in this course is the reaction phase, which can mislead the clinician into thinking the patient is improving. It is not recovery.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because a perforation that has stopped hurting sounds closed. Ask what the still-tender belly tells you about the peritoneum.

sure_note.text: You were sure the pain means the leak has closed; the peritoneum says otherwise.

say.text: Nothing has sealed. The lull follows chemical peritonitis and is followed by bacterial contamination, so the perforation is still open and needs urgent surgical review.
An immunosuppressed man has sudden epigastric pain with only mild, blunted peritoneal signs.
What is the safe next step?

choices.label: Image for perforation; mild signs do not exclude it
Observe overnight, since his signs are not board-like yet
Treat as dyspepsia, discharge with antacids and review

say.text: Yes. Steroids and age blunt peritoneal signs, so mild signs do not rule out a perforation.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because a rigid belly is the textbook sign, and his belly is not rigid. Ask whether the textbook sign is always present in this host.

sure_note.text: You were sure rigidity is the test; in this host it may never come.

say.text: Rigidity is a classic sign, but signs are blunted in the elderly and immunosuppressed. Waiting for board-like signs delays the diagnosis.
That choice is not right.
It is tempting because dyspepsia is common, and the pain sounds like it. Ask whether this host can hide a perforation behind mild signs.

sure_note.text: You were sure this is dyspepsia; mild signs do not settle it in this host.

say.text: Dyspepsia is a diagnosis of exclusion here, and this host can have a perforation with mild signs. Image first, then decide.
That is the end of the mixed quiz. Your reminder cards follow.

cards.q: Which wall of the first part of the duodenum perforates most often?
cards.a: The anterior wall, which faces the free belly. Posterior ulcers bleed by eroding the gastroduodenal artery.

cards.q: What is the commonest cause of pneumoperitoneum, and what is a Chilaiditi sign?
cards.a: Perforated peptic ulcer. Chilaiditi sign is colon between liver and diaphragm, a pseudo-pneumoperitoneum.

cards.q: What does the period of reaction mean?
cards.a: A lull after chemical peritonitis, before diffuse bacterial peritonitis. It is not recovery.

cards.q: First test versus most sensitive test for free gas?
cards.a: Erect chest X-ray is first; CT abdomen is the most sensitive and the choice when the film is equivocal.

cards.q: Does a clear erect film exclude perforation?
cards.a: No. Free gas shows in about three-quarters of perforations, so a clear film does not exclude one.

cards.q: What comes first in a shocked patient with peritonitis?
cards.a: Resuscitation: IV access, crystalloid and a nasogastric tube. Antibiotics and IV PPI start on diagnosis.
A selected stable patient whose perforation is contained and confirmed on a water-soluble contrast study.
